sec.title: Background and purpose
sec.p: Radiotherapy (RT) for breast cancer may increase atrial fibrillation (AF) risk. This study explored the association between RT and expression of AF-related genes in breast tumor tissues.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A total of 1094 breast cancer patients (RT group: 1020; non-RT group: 74) were included based on inclusion criteria. Clinical data and RNA-seq profiles (TPM) were retrieved. Six AF-related genes (MYBPC3, LMNA, PKP2, FAM189A2, KDM5B, MYL4) were analyzed. Gene expression was compared using Wilcoxon rank-sum test after Log2(TPM + 1) transformation. Subgroup analyses were conducted by AJCC stage (I–III), laterality (left/right), age (< 65/≥65 years), clinical subtype (Luminal, HER2-positive, Triple-negative), and PAM50 molecular subtype (Basal, Her2, LumA, LumB, Normal). Multivariate linear regression was applied to evaluate RT’s independent effect on gene expression.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In tumor tissues, expression levels of MYBPC3, LMNA, and MYL4 were significantly higher in the RT group compared to the non-RT group.Subgroup analysis revealed higher MYBPC3 expression in the RT group specifically in Stage III tumors, but lower expression in left-sided tumors and in patients < 65 years old. LMNA expression was higher in the RT group in Stage III tumors. MYL4 expression was higher in the RT group in Stage II tumors, in both left and right-sided tumors, and in both age groups (< 65 and ≥ 65 years). No significant differences were found across clinical or molecular subtypes for any gene.Multivariate regression confirmed RT as an independent predictor of increased MYL4 expression (β = 0.204), but not for MYBPC3 or LMNA expression. Sensitivity analysis in the 45–65 age subgroup supports the above findings.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Based on tumor tissue analysis, breast cancer radiotherapy is associated with altered expression of AF-related genes (particularly MYL4) in tumor tissues, suggesting a potential molecular link worthy of further exploration in relation to atrial fibrillation. These findings warrant future validation in cardiac or circulatory tissues.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Breast cancer is the malignant tumor with the highest incidence rate among women globally, and its incidence rate is increasing year by year, surpassing lung cancer to become the world’s largest cancer in 2020 [1]. Therefore, the prevention and treatment of breast cancer has become a major challenge in public health [2]. In recent years, with the advancement of diagnostic and therapeutic techniques, the survival rate of breast cancer patients has been significantly improved, and the survival period has been continuously prolonged, and the quality of their long-term survival and treatment-related long-term complications have received increasing attention. Radiation therapy (RT), as one of the core tools in the comprehensive treatment of breast cancer (especially for post-breast-conserving surgery and locally advanced patients), plays an irreplaceable role in reducing the local recurrence rate and improving the survival rate [3, 4]. However, it is worth noting that while RT brings significant survival benefits, its potential cardiovascular toxicity cannot be ignored [5]. Radiotherapy radiation inevitably affects part of the heart and adjacent macrovascular structures, which may lead to a series of delayed cardiovascular complications, including coronary artery disease [6], myocardial fibrosis [7], pericarditis [8], and cardiac arrhythmias [9, 10].

Among them, cardiac arrhythmias, especially Atrial Fibrillation (AF), have become the focus of research due to their high prevalence and significant clinical harm. Studies have shown that AF not only significantly increases the risk of stroke, heart failure, and death in patients, but also may interfere with the course of tumor therapy and impair the quality of patient survival [11]. Of concern, RT itself is also an important risk factor for AF in tumor patients [12]. Exposure to ionizing radiation increases the risk of vascular inflammation, promotes myocardial fibrosis, and increases the risk of heart failure and ischemic heart disease in a dose-dependent manner [12], all of which are established risk factors for AF.A cohort study by Guha et al. [13] of breast cancer patients demonstrated that radioactive particle implantation therapy, when compared to conventional external irradiation radiotherapy, was associated with a lower risk in terms of the development of AF, which was speculated to be It may be related to its lower radiation dose to the heart. Recent studies have further revealed that radiation-induced myocardial tissue damage [14] and electrophysiological remodeling may be an important pathological basis for the development of radiotherapy-associated AF [15], but the underlying molecular mechanisms have not been fully elucidated.

Notably, several genomics studies have found that aberrant expression of specific genes is closely associated with the development of AF.Choi et al. evaluated the impact of rare coding genetic variants on AF risk using the largest complex disease sequencing data available and found significant associations [16]. In addition, a study by Nathan Orr and Rima Arnaout et al. found that MYL4 mutations may be an important cause of atrial myopathy and arrhythmias by studying the genetics of familial AF in a patient with AF and his family members and constructing a corresponding zebrafish model [17]. Therefore, systematic exploration of AF-related gene expression changes during radiotherapy in breast cancer patients is of great significance for an in-depth understanding of the molecular mechanisms of radiotherapy-induced arrhythmias. With the rapid development of high-throughput sequencing technology and bioinformatics methods, analyzing the multi-omics data of breast cancer patients based on large-scale databases such as TCGA (The Cancer Genome Atlas) has become an effective way to reveal the molecular features of the disease development and its treatment-related complications. However, there is a relative paucity of studies on the association between breast cancer radiotherapy and AF-related gene expression.

Therefore, this study will be based on the TCGA-BRCA database, combined with patients’ clinical information and gene expression data, to investigate the expression characteristics of genes closely related to AF in breast cancer patients receiving radiotherapy or not. Based on the above, this study aims to reveal the molecular link between breast cancer radiotherapy and AF, to provide new theoretical basis and potential targeted intervention strategies for clinical prediction and prevention of radiotherapy-related arrhythmias, and thus to promote the overall prognosis and quality of life of breast cancer patients.

sec.title: Data sources
sec.p: The data for this study were obtained from the official database of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). We downloaded the clinical data of 1098 breast cancer patients from TCGA, including key variables such as patient ID, gender, age, AJCC pathological stage, tumor affected side (left/right), treatment type (including radiotherapy information), as well as tumor subtypes (Luminal, HER2-positive, Triple-negative) and PAM50 molecular subtypes. Meanwhile, we downloaded gene expression data (RNA-seq) from 1231 patients, covering both tumor tissue and adjacent normal tissue samples. After a rigorous data quality control and matching process, we finally retained the gene expression data of 1084 breast cancer patients with complete clinical information and the corresponding 1230 patient tissues. These expression data included TPM (Transcripts Per Million)values for 1117 tumor tissue samples and 113 adjacent normal tissue samples.

sec.title: AF-related gene screening
sec.p: To investigate the potential association between breast cancer treatment and atrial fibrillation risk, we first screened existing literature and disease databases to identify genes with established significant associations with atrial fibrillation occurrence, progression, and genetic risk. Through systematic retrieval and evaluation, we ultimately identified six core candidate genes: MYBPC3, LMNA, PKP2, FAM189A2, KDM5B, and MYL4. These genes function in multiple key pathways involved in the pathophysiology of atrial fibrillation, including myocardial structural maintenance, ion channel regulation, and epigenetic modifications [16–18]. The known functions of candidate genes, supporting evidence for their association with atrial fibrillation, and key references are detailed in Table S1.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics were performed for demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population. Continuous variables were described using mean ± standard deviation (Mean ± SD) or median and interquartile range [Median (IQR)], and comparisons between groups were made using the independent samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U-test, respectively. Categorical variables were described by frequency and percentage [n (%)], and comparisons between groups were made using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. For comparison of gene expression differences between groups, the independent samples t-test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test was employed. The RT group was defined by whether one or more of the patients’ multiple treatment regimens involved radiotherapy, and vice versa for the non-RT group, and the differences in baseline characteristics between the RT and non-RT groups were compared.

Gene expression data (TPM) were first log2-transformed (log2(TPM + 1)) to satisfy the prerequisite assumptions for subsequent statistical analyses and improve data distribution. The primary analysis focused on tumor tissue samples. Expression level differences between the RT group and non-RT group were compared for six candidate genes (MYBPC3, LMNA, PKP2, FAM189A2, KDM5B, MYL4). For genes showing significant expression differences (P < 0.05) between the RT and non-RT groups in the overall tumor tissue analysis, we further explored the heterogeneity of this expression difference across the following clinical subgroups: Cancer Stage subgroups (normal tissue, Stage I, Stage II, Stage III); Tumor Laterality subgroups (left-sided and right-sided tumors); age subgroups (< 65 years, ≥ 65 years); Clinical Subtype subgroups (luminal, HER2-positive, triple-negative); and PAM50 Subtype subgroups (basal-like, HER2-overexpressing, LumA, LumB, normal-like). When performing subgroup analyses, multiple comparisons were accounted for to control the risk of false-positive results. The false discovery rate (FDR) method was applied to adjust P-values for subgroups comprising more than two categories, including the Cancer Stage subgroups, Clinical Subtype subgroups, and PAM50 Subtype subgroups. No corrections were applied to subgroups containing only two categories (Tumor Laterality subgroups and age subgroups).

In addition, to assess whether radiotherapy (RT) was an independent predictor of high expression of AF-related genes, we further performed multiple linear regression analyses for genes with significant differences (MYBPC3, LMNA, MYL4). The Log2 (TPM + 1) expression values of the genes were used as the dependent variables, and the independent variables included radiotherapy (yes/no), age group (< 65 years/≥65 years), Cancer Stage (stage I/II/III), and Tumor Laterality (left/right).

Additionally, to assess the robustness of study findings in the overall population and address potential bias arising from significant imbalance between the radiotherapy and non-radiotherapy groups, we conducted a sensitivity analysis. Specifically, we restricted the analysis to a clinically relevant and more homogeneous subgroup: tumor patients aged 45–65 years. This age range encompasses the peak incidence of breast cancer while excluding younger patients (< 45 years) who may exhibit distinct tumor biology and older patients (≥ 65 years) whose gene expression patterns could be confounded by age-related comorbidities. We performed multivariate linear regression analysis on candidate genes in tumors from patients within this age range, using Log2(TPM + 1) expression values as the dependent variable. The regression model included the following independent variables: radiotherapy (yes/no), Tumor Laterality (left/right), and Cancer Stage (I/II/III). The results enabled us to assess whether the associations observed in the overall population remained valid within a more clearly defined clinical subgroup.

All statistical analyses for this study were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27 as well as R Studio version 4.2.1, and all tests were two-sided and considered statistically significant at P < 0.05.

sec.title: Baseline characteristics of the study population
sec.p: A total of 1094 breast cancer patients were included in this study, of whom 1020 (93.2%) received radiotherapy. Patients were categorized into RT group (n = 1020) and non-RT group (n = 74) according to whether they received radiotherapy or not. The baseline characteristics of the patients in the two groups were compared as shown in Table 1. There were significant differences in the age distribution between the two groups, both in continuous (P = 0.010) and categorical variables (P < 0.001). Specifically, patients in the RT group were younger (58.15 ± 12.99 years) compared to the non-RT group (62.59 ± 14.91 years), and a higher proportion of patients in the RT group were under 65 years old (70.00% vs. 51.35%). No statistically significant differences were observed in gender distribution (P = 0.570), Tumor Laterality (P = 0.601), clinical subtypes (P = 0.858), or PAM50 molecular subtypes (P = 0.176) between the two groups. While the non-RT group contained more normal tissue samples (29.17% vs. 4.15%), the overall distribution of cancer stages (Stages I, II, III, and Others) did not differ significantly between the RT and non-RT groups after statistical testing (P = 0.820).

sec.title: Differential expression analysis of AF-related genes between RT and non-RT groups
sec.p: The results of the differential expression analysis of the candidate genes between the RT and non-RT groups showed that: In the tumor tissues, the expression levels (log₂(TPM + 1)) of MYBPC3, LMNA and MYL4genes were significantly higher in the RT group than in the non-RT group (Fig. 1A–C). The expression differences of the remaining three candidate genes (PKP2, FAM189A2, and KDM5B) between the two groups were not statistically significant (Fig. 1D–F).

caption.p: Differential expression of candidate genes between RT group and Non-RT group. ns means not statistically significant; *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01

sec.title: Clinical subgroup heterogeneity analysis of differentially expressed genes in the RT group
sec.p: Subgroup analysis was performed on genes showing significant intergroup differential expression. First, subgroup analysis based on BRCA staging was conducted (Fig. 2A–C): In stage III tumor tissues, the expression level of the MYBPC3 gene (log2(TPM + 1)) was significantly higher in the radiotherapy group than in the non-radiotherapy group, but this difference disappeared after FDR correction (Fig. 2A). In stage III tumor tissues, the LMNA gene expression level (log2(TPM + 1)) was significantly higher in the radiotherapy group than in the non-radiotherapy group, and this difference remained significant after FDR correction (Fig. 2B). In stage II tumor tissues, the expression level of the MYL4 gene (log2(TPM + 1)) was significantly higher in the radiotherapy group than in the non-radiotherapy group, but this difference disappeared after FDR correction (Fig. 2C).

Second, subgroup analysis was performed based on the affected side of the tumor (Fig. 2D–F): in the left tumor tissues, the expression level of MYBPC3 gene (log₂(TPM + 1)) was significantly lower in the RT group than in the non-RT group (Fig. 2D). In both left and right tumor tissues, the expression level of MYL4 gene (log₂(TPM + 1)) was significantly higher in the RT group than in the non-RT group (Fig. 2F).

In addition, subgroup analyses were performed based on patient age (Fig. 2G–I): in tumor tissues of patients younger than 65 years old, the expression levels (log₂(TPM + 1)) of MYBPC3 gene were significantly lower in the RT group than in the non-RT group, while the expression levels of MYL4 gene were significantly higher in the RT group (Fig. 2G–I). In the tumor tissues of patients aged 65 years and above, the expression levels of MYL4 gene were significantly higher in the RT group than in the non-RT group (Fig. 2H, I).

Furthermore, subgroup analyses were conducted based on clinical subtype (Fig. 2J–L) and detailed molecular subtype (Fig. 2M–O). No statistically significant differences in the expression levels (log₂(TPM + 1)) of the three genes (MYBPC3, LMNA, and MYL4) were observed between the RT and non-RT groups across these clinical and molecular subtypes.

A–C differential expression across tumor stages; D–F differential expression by tumor laterality; G–I differential expression across age groups; J–L differential expression by clinical subtype; M–O differential expression by detailed molecular subtype. Only genes showing significant differential expression in the overall cohort are displayed. *P < 0.05; #FDR < 0.05; ns: not statistically significant. Luminal (clinical subtype): A breast cancer subtype characterized by expression of hormone receptors (ER + and/or PR+); HER2_positive: Breast cancer characterized by overexpression of the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) protein; TNBC (Triple-Negative Breast Cancer): Breast cancer that lacks expression of estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2; LumA (Luminal A): A molecular subtype defined by PAM50 assay, typically ER + and/or PR+, HER2-; Luminal B (HER2-): ER + and/or PR+, HER2-; Luminal B (HER2+): ER + and/or PR+, HER2+. Among these, the cancer staging subgroup, clinical subtype subgroup, and PAM50 subtype subgroup underwent FDR correction

sec.title: Independent prediction of AF-related gene expression by RT
sec.p: The results of the multiple linear regression analysis. Figure 3 showed that in Model 1 (crude model), radiotherapy was significantly associated with elevated MYL4 expression (log₂(TPM + 1); β [95% CI]: 0.182 [0.028–0.336], P = 0.021). After adjustment for age(< 65 years/≥65 years), diagnoses laterality(Left/Right), pathologic stage(stage I/II/III) in Model 2, radiotherapy remained significantly associated with elevated MYL4 expression (log₂(TPM + 1); β [95% CI]: 0.204 [0.037–0.372], P = 0.017). In contrast, no significant associations were observed between radiotherapy and the expression of MYBPC3 (Model 1: β [95% CI ]: 0.069 [-0.043-0.181], P = 0.225; Model 2: β [95% CI]: 0.059 [-0.033-0.152], P = 0.206) or LMNA (Model 1: β [95% CI]: 0.268 [-0.196-0.732], P = 0.255; Model 2: β [95% CI]: 0.374 [-0.124-0.872], P = 0.139) in either crude or adjusted models.

caption.p: Multivariable Linear Regression Analysis of Radiotherapy as an Independent Predictor for Atrial Fibrillation-Related Gene Expression. Model 1: crude model; Model 2: Adjusted for Age(< 65 years/≥65 years), Diagnoses Laterality(Left/Right), Pathologic Stage(stage I/II/III)

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis
sec.p: A sensitivity analysis was conducted in tumor patients aged 45–65 years (n = 550), with results shown in Fig. 4. After adjusting for tumor Diagnoses Laterality(Left/Right) and Pathologic Stage(stage I/II/III), radiotherapy remained significantly associated with elevated MYL4 expression (β = 0.154, 95% CI: 0.024–0.284, P = 0.020). Conversely, radiotherapy remained significantly associated with both MYBPC3 expression (β = −0.002, 95% CI: −0.065 to 0.062, P = 0.958) and LMNA expression (β = 0.118, 95% CI: −0.194 to 0.429, P = 0.459). These findings were consistent with those observed in the overall population.

Model 1: crude model; Model 2: Adjusted for Diagnoses Laterality (Left/Right), Pathologic Stage (stage I/II/III)

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study represents the first systematic analysis of the association between breast cancer radiotherapy and the expression profiles of key atrial fibrillation (AF) risk genes, based on the TCGA-BRCA database. Results revealed that in tumor tissues, the RT group exhibited significantly higher expression levels of MYBPC3, LMNA, and MYL4 genes compared to the non-RT group in initial differential expression analysis, with these differences showing heterogeneity across specific clinical subgroups. However, multiple linear regression analysis adjusted for potential confounders indicated that radiotherapy was an independent predictor of MYL4 upregulation, but not of MYBPC3 or LMNA upregulation. Sensitivity analyses in the 45–65 age cohort supported this finding. This significant discovery suggests radiotherapy may contribute to atrial fibrillation development primarily through direct or indirect regulation of MYL4 expression. Notably, other candidate genes (PKP2, FAM189A2, KDM5B) showed no significant differences between groups, indicating radiotherapy’s selective impact on atrial fibrillation-associated genes.

MYL4 is a myosin light chain specifically expressed in atrial muscle and is directly involved in the assembly of the myocardial contractile apparatus and calcium regulation [19]. Functional mutations in this gene have been shown to cause familial atrial cardiomyopathy and AF [17]. In this study, we found that MYL4 expression was significantly upregulated in tumor tissues of breast cancer patients in the RT group. Subgroup analyses indicated that this upregulation was consistent in both left and right-sided tumors, as well as in patients both younger and older than 65 years. Critically, the association between radiotherapy and elevated MYL4 expression remained significant after adjusting for age, laterality, and pathologic stage. This finding differs from observations in some genetic disease models, such as the study by Chen et al. where MYL4 expression was downregulated in an atrial cardiomyopathy mouse model [20]. An American study showed that the incidence of new-onset atrial fibrillation during the 1-year period of diagnosis was about twice as high in breast cancer patients as in the cancer-free population [13]. Another study showed that ionizing radiation inevitably leads to cardiomyocyte damage during radiotherapy, especially for left-sided breast tumors [21]. However, recent studies have provided a key explanation for the phenomenon of up-regulation of MYL4 expression. Berber et al. found that MYL4 was a consistently highly expressed gene in the left atrium and peripheral blood of patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) by RNA-seq analysis, suggesting that it may be directly involved in the pathogenesis of AF [22]. Zhong et al. demonstrated that overexpression of MYL4 by adenoviral vectors significantly ameliorated MYL4-deficient atrial fibrosis and autophagic flow disturbance in rats, confirming that MYL4 upregulation has a cardioprotective effect [23]. Notably, while tumor tissue expression alone cannot directly indicate cardiac effects, it is possible that tumor cells may secrete paracrine factors, inflammatory cytokines, or exosomes into the circulation that indirectly influence cardiac electrophysiology or remodeling. For example, RT-induced systemic inflammation or oxidative stress could potentially trigger myocardial stress responses, which in turn may upregulate atrial contractile proteins such as MYL4 [23]. These potential indirect mechanisms provide a biologically plausible pathway linking tumor gene expression changes to cardiac consequences, although functional validation in ex vivo or in vivo models is required. These potential indirect mechanisms provide a biologically plausible pathway linking tumor gene expression changes to cardiac consequences, although functional validation in ex vivo or in vivo models is required.

The LMNA gene encodes a structural protein of the nuclear fiber layer, which is essential for maintaining nuclear stability, DNA repair, and regulation of gene expression [24, 25]. In this study, we observed that LMNA expression in the RT group was significantly elevated in the overall cohort and Stage III patients, and was particularly prominent in older patients ≥ 65 years of age. This phenomenon may reflect radiotherapy-induced nuclear structural damage, DNA repair stress, or premature aging-like changes in cardiomyocytes [14] Although no literature related to breast cancer radiotherapy affecting LMNA gene expression has been found yet, the high LMNA expression in the RT group (especially in stage III and elderly patients) supports the hypothesis of radiation-accelerated myocardial fibrosis, which is consistent with the radiation dose-dependent cardiotoxicity mechanism proposed by Guha et al. [13]. In addition, Din et al. demonstrated that ATM inhibition significantly enhanced radiosensitivity both in vitro and in vivo [26]. ATM activation may affect the p53 transcription factor [27], which regulates LMNA expression [28]. In addition, abnormal accumulation of LMNA was found to activate the downstream TGF-β pathway [29–31], promoting extracellular matrix deposition, which ultimately leads to structural remodeling of the atria and increased heterogeneity of electrical conduction, constituting the pathological basis for the development of AF [31]. Elderly patients are more susceptible to myocardial fibrosis after radiotherapy due to their inherent aging-associated nuclear membrane fragility, which provides a molecular explanation for the high risk of AF after radiotherapy in elderly breast cancer patients.

MYBPC3 is a key structural protein of myofibroblasts and is involved in the regulation of myocardial contractility [32]. Although its variants are mostly seen in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, recent studies have suggested that it is associated with AF risk [16]. In this study, we found that MYBPC3 expression was significantly elevated in the RT group in the overall cohort, Stage II/III and left-sided breast cancer patients, and the difference was more significant in patients < 65 years old. It has been shown that MYBPC3 gene mutations promote myocardial fibrosis by activating the NF-κB/TGF-β1/HIF-1α axis in fibroblasts and driving glycolytic metabolic reprogramming [33]. In contrast, Chargari et al. found that radiohepatic injury in rats was transduced through the TGF-β1/Smads signaling pathway [34]. Therefore, radiotherapy may have led to the upregulation of MYBPC3 expression through DNA damage or ROS activation of NF-κB, which promotes TGF-β1 expression, and then induces myocardial fibroblast activation, but this needs to be verified by further mechanistic studies. In addition, subgroup analysis performed in this study revealed significantly high expression of MYBPC3 in the RT group of left-sided tumors, which is consistent with the results of other studies. Studies have shown that the 15-year incidence of cardiovascular event involvement in patients with left-sided breast cancer treated with radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery was 7.6%, which was 1.1% higher than that of those who were not treated with radiotherapy [35]. Therefore, radiotherapy for patients with left-sided breast cancer needs to be highly alert to the potential risk of cardiovascular toxicity while pursuing local control of the tumor. Studies have shown that coronary artery injury may be a key link in the increased incidence of cardiac disease after radiotherapy, and it is also a research hotspot for cardioprotection in breast cancer radiotherapy in recent years [36, 37]. MYBPC3 functional alterations, while primarily affecting the heart, may indirectly influence the breast tumor microenvironment through systemic calcium signaling dysregulation [38] and EGFR/IGF1R-mediated cardiac dysfunction [39]. Indirectly, systemic oxidative stress or pro-fibrotic factors released from irradiated tumor tissue could affect myocardial fibroblasts and promote remodeling, providing a potential mechanistic link between RT and AF risk beyond direct cardiac radiation exposure [33]. In conclusion, it is suggested that MYBPC3 may be a molecular bridge connecting radiotherapy-coronary microinjury-arrhythmia, but further studies are needed to demonstrate this.

Our study further evaluated the independent impact of radiotherapy on atrial fibrillation-associated genes through multivariate linear regression analysis, after adjusting for potential confounding factors such as age, tumor lateralization, and pathological staging. Results demonstrated that radiotherapy was an independent predictor of elevated MYL4 expression (adjusted β = 0.204, P = 0.017). This finding suggests that differences in MYL4 expression observed across the general population may be independent of confounding factors such as age, tumor location, or disease stage. However, for MYBPC3 and LMNA, although univariate analysis showed higher expression in the radiotherapy group, multivariate models did not reveal an independent statistical association between radiotherapy and their expression levels (MYBPC3 adjusted β = 0.059, P = 0.206; LMNA adjusted β = 0.374, P = 0.139). This suggests that the observed differences in MYBPC3 and LMNA expression in the overall analysis may be partially confounded by clinical characteristics such as age and tumor stage. Collectively, this study indicates that after adjusting for key clinical variables, radiotherapy is independently associated with the upregulation of certain atrial fibrillation-related genes (e.g., MYL4) in tumor tissue. This finding provides clues for further exploration of the systemic biological effects of radiotherapy. It is important to note that this analysis is based on tumor tissue data and is subject to limitations such as sample size imbalance between cohorts. Therefore, the above association should be considered a preliminary finding, and its validity and clinical significance in cardiac tissue require validation in future studies.

It should be noted that the baseline expression levels (TPM) of MYBPC3 and MYL4 in tumor tissues were relatively low in this study. This aligns with their known biological characteristics: MYL4 is an atrial-specific myosin light chain [17], while MYBPC3 is also a protein primarily expressed in cardiac muscle [40]. Their background expression in breast epithelial cells or tumor cells may be limited. This suggests caution should be exercised when interpreting the absolute magnitude of their expression changes. However, the core focus of this study lies in exploring the association between radiotherapy and trends in gene expression changes, rather than the absolute levels of baseline expression. The statistically significant relative upregulation of MYL4 observed in the radiotherapy group may reflect a potentially cross-tissue, systemic stress or signaling response triggered by radiotherapy [23]. That is, even if the signal strength is weak, the directionality and consistency of the change warrant attention and provide potential clues for subsequent research. Of course, whether these low-level signal changes in tumor tissue truly reflect corresponding gene expression alterations in the heart, and whether such alterations possess actual pathophysiological functions, must be definitively determined through direct validation in cardiac tissue samples or experimental models. Therefore, the current findings should be regarded as preliminary, suggestive discoveries, whose biological and clinical significance requires further elucidation through subsequent studies.

Overall, although our study is based on tumor tissue analysis, the results indicate increased expression of certain genes associated with atrial fibrillation. This suggests that radiotherapy may influence cardiac electrical activity and structure through systemic or indirect mechanisms. Radiotherapy-induced systemic inflammation and oxidative stress can trigger the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 from tumors and immune cells into the circulation [41]. These mediators may activate signaling pathways like NF-κB in cardiomyocytes [42], promoting fibrosis and ion channel remodeling. This ultimately damages cardiomyocytes and vascular endothelial cells, leading to atrial fibrillation. Additionally, radiotherapy alters the composition of tumor-secreted exosomes, which carry miRNAs, proteins, and metabolites [43]. Once in the bloodstream, they can be taken up by cardiac cells, potentially regulating gene expression and cellular functions associated with atrial fibrillation [44, 45]. Collectively, these mechanisms reflect the cardiac risks posed by radiotherapy, which may not solely result from direct cardiac irradiation but could also arise indirectly through signals released by tumors. Future studies should integrate cardiac imaging, circulating extracellular vesicle (CEV) analysis, and long-term follow-up to further validate these hypotheses in both experimental and clinical settings.

So far, this study has the following advantages. First, this study is the first to systematically resolve the association between breast cancer radiotherapy and AF risk gene expression profiles based on the TCGA-BRCA database, which fills a gap in the field; second, this study used strictly quality-controlled RNA-seq data (n = 1094, 1020 cases in the RT group/74 cases in the non-RT group), which provided sufficient statistical validity; meanwhile, the set of candidate genes of the present study originated from the latest high-quality genomics studies, ensuring strong association with AF pathomechanisms; finally, this study was analyzed by subgroup stratification (staging/lateralization/age) and multivariate regression modeling, thus effectively revealing the independent predictive role of radiotherapy. Of course, this study also has several important limitations. First, the study lacks clinical outcome data, such as atrial fibrillation incidence, which precludes direct assessment of the prognostic value of the identified molecular markers.​ Second, gene expression analysis was based entirely on breast tumor tissue rather than atrial myocardial tissue, limiting direct interpretation of results in terms of cardiac pathology. Third, the severe imbalance in sample size between the radiotherapy group and the non-radiotherapy group may affect the stability of statistical inferences. Furthermore, the study lacks cardiac radiation dose data, preventing the establishment of a dose-response relationship. Finally, the retrospective design may introduce unmeasured confounding factors. These limitations suggest that the current findings are primarily hypothesis-generating, proposing a potential molecular link, and their clinical relevance​ requires further validation in prospective studies incorporating cardiac tissue analysis and AF incidence data.

sec.title: Clinical significance and future directions
sec.p: This study suggests that radiotherapy may contribute to atrial fibrillation risk by upregulating gene expression of MYL4 and others, providing new molecular clues for investigating the mechanisms of radiotherapy-related arrhythmias. Future studies should integrate cardiac imaging, plasma biomarkers, and long-term follow-up data to further validate the association between these gene expression alterations and clinical atrial fibrillation events. In clinical practice, enhanced electrocardiographic monitoring and cardiovascular risk assessment should be implemented for breast cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy (particularly those with left-sided tumors and elderly patients), alongside exploration of individualized radiotherapy planning and cardiac protection strategies.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Overall, our study revealed an association between breast cancer radiotherapy and altered expression of certain atrial fibrillation-related genes (e.g., MYL4) in tumor tissues. This suggests that radiotherapy may induce specific molecular changes within the tumor microenvironment, providing a novel molecular perspective for exploring its potential systemic or distant cardiac effects.​ Future studies should validate these gene alterations at the cardiac tissue or systemic levels and evaluate future research to evaluate their biological significance and potential mechanisms in conjunction with clinical AF outcomes.
